title: Chat Storage & Delivery
description: Design store-and-forward messaging with Cassandra for write-optimized storage, delivery receipts, push notifications via APNs/FCM, and offline message queuing.

segments.text: Chat uses store-and-forward architecture. The sender sends a message to the server, the server stores it persistently, then forwards it to the recipient. If the recipient is offline, the message waits in storage until they reconnect. WhatsApp stores over a hundred billion messages per day using this pattern.

Chat messages are write-heavy and append-only — you never update a message. Cassandra is ideal: it's designed for high write throughput with its LSM-tree storage engine. Partition by conversation ID, cluster by timestamp. This gives you O(1) writes and range-scan reads — fetch the last fifty messages in a conversation efficiently.

The message delivery flow: sender sends via WebSocket to a chat server, chat server writes to Cassandra and looks up the recipient's connection. If online, push immediately via their WebSocket. Acknowledge back to the sender with a 'delivered' receipt. The entire path should complete in under one hundred milliseconds for a good user experience.

Delivery receipts have three states: sent — server received the message, delivered — recipient's device received it, read — recipient opened the conversation. Each state requires a separate acknowledgment flowing back to the sender. WhatsApp's blue checks implement exactly this three-state receipt system with server-side tracking.

When the recipient is offline, trigger a push notification. Apple's APNs and Google's FCM are the delivery channels. Your server sends a notification payload to APNs or FCM, which delivers it to the device. Critical detail: never put message content in the push notification payload — it traverses third-party servers. Just send 'new message' and let the app fetch the content securely.

A user has been offline for two weeks. They have three thousand unread messages across fifty conversations. When they come back online, how do you sync their messages without overwhelming their device or your servers?
segments.thought_prompt: How would you sync 3,000 unread messages to a device reconnecting after 2 weeks offline?

segments.text: The offline message queue stores pending messages per user. When the user reconnects, the server pushes messages in chronological order with pagination — fifty messages at a time. Use a cursor-based approach: the device tracks the last received message ID and requests everything after it. This handles both short and long offline periods gracefully.

Online presence — showing who's online — seems simple but is expensive at scale. With five hundred million users, tracking presence changes generates massive event volume. WhatsApp only shows last-seen timestamps, not real-time presence, because real-time presence for a user with one thousand contacts means broadcasting to one thousand connections on every status change.

Message ordering within a conversation must be preserved. Use server-assigned sequence numbers per conversation — not timestamps, because clock skew between devices can reorder messages. Each conversation has a monotonically increasing counter. The server assigns the next sequence number on receive, guaranteeing consistent ordering for all participants.

Design the storage and delivery layer for a chat system handling one billion messages per day with sub-one-hundred-millisecond delivery latency for online users. What's your data model, server architecture, and sync strategy?
segments.thought_prompt: Design chat storage and delivery for 1B messages/day with sub-100ms delivery. Full architecture.

segments.text: Chat storage and delivery combines write-optimized storage in Cassandra, WebSocket-based real-time delivery, three-state delivery receipts, push notifications for offline users, and cursor-based offline sync. The key insight: separate the storage path from the delivery path. Store once, deliver through whichever channel the recipient is reachable on.
